113.title: When you stop, and start again
113.hook: two weeks of all five, then one missed, then none: the deeds most loved are the steady ones, even if small
113.howItsDone: Muslims hold the five daily prayers to be a duty; when someone has drifted from them, many imams and teachers advise coming back prayer by prayer, keeping each one steady, and asking a trusted scholar about making up what was missed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fajr, the whole dawn prayer, every piece in order, takbir to taslim. Your line was the whole thing. Today, what happens after you've learned it, and then stop.

Ramadan, or a new year, or a hard week, and the prayers come back. Two weeks, all five. Then one gets missed. Then two. Then the adhan sounds from a phone across the room, there's a sting of guilt, and the prayer still doesn't happen. A few months later, the whole thing starts again. Underneath sits one quiet question: am I a bad Muslim? Today, what the tradition says to someone stuck in that loop.
screen: `TWO WEEKS, ALL FIVE.` → `THEN ONE MISSED. THEN NONE.` → `AM I A BAD MUSLIM?`

segments.voice: First, the plain part. Across the major schools, the five daily prayers are a duty, not an extra. This lesson doesn't soften that. It's about how people get back to them. Aisha, the Prophet's wife, reported a saying that speaks straight to the loop. The Prophet ﷺ was asked which deeds are most loved by Allah. The most constant ones, he said, even if small. In Arabic, wa in qall: even if it is little. And when he began something, she added, he kept it up. Not the heroic week: the thing that keeps going. That's why many teachers, when someone has drifted, don't say all five tomorrow or don't bother. They say: pray the next one. Guard it. Then add another. The goal stays five; the way back is one at a time. If there's a long stretch of missed prayers behind you, scholars differ on how to make them up; that's a question for a teacher you trust, not a reason to wait. Then there's the voice that says you've already failed. Camp two named it: waswas, the whisper. One of its oldest tricks is telling a person the door has shut. A saying the Prophet reported from Allah, in Bukhari, says the opposite: whoever draws near to Me by a hand's span, I draw near by an arm's length; whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running. And it's fine to ask for help with the praying itself. The Prophet told the companion Mu'adh that he loved him, then taught him to say at the end of every prayer: O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You, and to worship You well.
screen: `THE DUTY IS FIVE, PLAINLY.` · `MOST LOVED: THE STEADY ONES, EVEN IF SMALL.` · `PRAY THE NEXT ONE. GUARD IT. ADD ONE.` · `COME WALKING, AND HE COMES RUNNING.`

segments.voice: If you pray, choose just the next prayer, the one coming, and decide only that one, not the whole week; if you've been away a while, picture making wudu for it, and let that be enough. If you don't pray, choose one small good thing you once kept up and let slide, and picture doing it once more. Breathe out the guilt; breathe in the next one.
Adwamuha. The most constant of deeds, even if small: what the Prophet said Allah loves most.
Your line: small, steady, and back again. The door hasn't shut. Day one hundred thirteen.

114.title: Subhanallah, thirty-three
114.hook: glory be to Allah, for what is beyond everything
114.howItsDone: After the obligatory prayers many Muslims say subhanallah thirty-three times, then alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar, counting on the fingers or on prayer beads, and they say subhanallah through the day at anything awe-inspiring.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adwamuha, even if it is little: the steady deeds are the most loved. Your line was small, steady, and back again. Today, one of the steadiest small things there is. Day one hundred fourteen.

A sunset over the water, and someone on the sand whispers: subhanallah. A baby's tiny hand closes around a finger: subhanallah. A crazy coincidence, a near-miss on the highway, a mountain out of a plane window. It's the word Muslims reach for when something is too big, too beautiful or too strange for ordinary words. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim sets it after every prayer, thirty-three times, counted out quietly.
screen: `A SUNSET, A BABY'S HAND.` → `TOO BIG FOR ORDINARY WORDS.` → `THIRTY-THREE, AFTER EVERY PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Subhanallah means glory be to Allah, and saying it is called tasbih. The root underneath, s-b-h, is the one the Qur'an uses for the sun and moon, each floating in its orbit. Some readers hear that picture inside the word: something moving far off, out of reach. The classical meaning is simpler and bigger: subhanallah declares God far above any flaw, any limit, anything a person could imagine. That's why it fits the sunset. The sunset is beautiful, and the One behind it is beyond even that. The Qur'an says, in Surah al-Isra, that the seven heavens and the earth and everything in them glorify Him, and there's nothing that doesn't hymn His praise, but people don't understand their glorifying. So in the tradition, the whole world is already saying subhanallah. The one praying is just joining in. After the prayer, there's a set. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says: whoever glorifies Allah thirty-three times after every prayer, and praises Him thirty-three times, and says Allahu akbar thirty-three times, and completes the hundred with there is no god but Allah alone, has their sins forgiven, even if they were like the foam on the sea. Tasbih is the first thirty-three. How do people count? A hadith in Tirmidhi tells the women to count on their fingertips, because the fingers will be asked, and made to speak; many use the joints of the right hand. A string of prayer beads is often called a tasbih, too, named after the word it counts.
screen: `A ROOT THE QUR'AN USES FOR ORBITS.` · `FAR ABOVE ANY FLAW.` · `THE HEAVENS ALREADY SAY IT.` · `THIRTY-THREE, THEN THIRTY-THREE.` · then, large: `THE BEADS ARE NAMED FOR THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Rest your right hand, palm up, and touch each joint with your thumb, one count each: fifteen joints is one pass, so go twice and add three. If you pray, say subhanallah softly on each count, not rushing; if not, say the word glory, or simply count, and on each count picture something beautiful you've seen this week. At thirty-three, let the hand rest.
Tasbih. Saying subhanallah, glory be to Allah, far above anything; thirty-three times after the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: glory. A sky, a face, a kindness: now there's a word for it. Day one hundred fourteen, counted.

115.title: "My iman is low"
115.hook: Hanzalah feared he'd become a hypocrite because his faith faded at home; the Prophet ﷺ said: an hour, and an hour
115.howItsDone: Muslims often speak of iman rising and falling; in a low stretch many keep up small remembrance, a little Qur'an and good company, and many imams now also encourage seeing a doctor or counselor when the low is heavy or won't lift.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tasbih, subhanallah, the word the whole world is already saying. Your line was glory. Today, the days when even one word feels far away.

A man walks through Medina saying, to no one in particular: Hanzalah has become a hypocrite. He means himself. Abu Bakr stops him. What are you saying? Hanzalah explains. When he sits with the Prophet ﷺ, hearing about the Garden and the Fire, it's as if he can see them. Then he goes home, to his wife, his children, his fields, and much of it slips away. The feeling is gone, and it frightens him. Today: what the Prophet told him.
screen: `HANZALAH HAS BECOME A HYPOCRITE.` → `WITH THE PROPHET, AS IF HE COULD SEE.` → `AT HOME, IT FADES.`

segments.voice: Abu Bakr's answer is the first surprise. By Allah, he says, I feel the same. The two of them go to the Prophet together, and Hanzalah says it again. The Prophet hears him out, then says, in Sahih Muslim: by the One in whose hand my soul is, if you stayed always as you are with me, and in remembrance, the angels would shake your hands in your beds and on your roads. But, Hanzalah: sa'atan wa sa'atan. An hour, and an hour. He says it three times. Muslims today have a phrase for what Hanzalah felt: my iman is low. You met iman on day five, a faith the Qur'an speaks of as growing. What grows can dip. The hadith doesn't call the dip hypocrisy; it treats it as being human: hours of nearness, and hours of the kitchen, the children and the fields. A report in later collections, which scholars grade differently, says faith wears out in the heart the way a garment wears out, so ask Allah to renew it. The Qur'an says: “Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!” Not a grand gesture. A word. Subhanallah, once, in the car. Many people feel the dip most right after Ramadan, when the month's high fades. Said gently: a dry stretch is one thing. If the low is heavy and won't lift, if sleep or hope are slipping, or if you've had thoughts of not being here, that's more than iman, and it deserves real help: a doctor, a counselor, someone you trust. In the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
screen: `BY ALLAH, I FEEL THE SAME.` · `AN HOUR, AND AN HOUR.` · `WHAT GROWS CAN DIP. A WORD BRINGS IT BACK.` · `IF IT WON'T LIFT: REAL HELP, 988.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow; no high is required. If you pray, say one word of remembrance on each breath out, subhanallah or alhamdulillah, like leaving a small light on in an empty room; if you don't, notice one thing you're grateful for. If the words feel hollow, say them anyway, gently, and let that be today's hour.
Sa'atan wa sa'atan. An hour, and an hour: the Prophet's answer to Hanzalah, that faith has its hours of nearness and its ordinary hours. Today's word.
Your line: an hour, and an hour. A low hour isn't the end of the story. Day one hundred fifteen.

116.title: Allahu akbar, thirty-four
116.hook: the Prophet ﷺ taught this set to his daughter Fatimah instead of a servant (Bukhari)
116.howItsDone: Many Muslims say Allahu akbar thirty-four times, with subhanallah and alhamdulillah thirty-three times each, when going to bed, following the set taught to Fatimah, and a similar hundred after the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sa'atan wa sa'atan, the Prophet's answer to Hanzalah when faith faded at home. Your line was an hour, and an hour. Today, a hundred words for the tired hours.
screen: `SA'ATAN WA SA'ATAN — AN HOUR, AND AN HOUR.`

segments.voice: Think of the most tired you've ever been from work with your hands. Moving house. A double shift. A newborn at three in the morning. Now picture a young woman in Medina, her hands blistered from turning a stone hand mill every day, grinding grain for bread, and from hauling water. She's the Prophet's ﷺ youngest daughter, Fatimah. She hears that some servants have come to Medina, and she goes to her father to ask for one. Just one. Today: what he gave her instead.
screen: `BLISTERED HANDS.` → `A STONE HAND MILL.` → `SHE ASKS FOR ONE SERVANT.`

segments.voice: The story is in Bukhari and Muslim, told by her husband Ali. Fatimah went to the Prophet's house, but he wasn't there, so she told his wife Aisha why she'd come. That night, after Fatimah and Ali had gone to bed, the Prophet came to their house. They started to get up. Stay where you are, he said, and sat down between them. Ali remembered the coolness of his feet. Then: shall I tell you something better than what you asked for? When you go to bed, say Allahu akbar thirty-four times, subhanallah thirty-three times, and alhamdulillah thirty-three times. That is better for you than a servant. A hundred in all. It's a strange answer, if you're tired. She asked for help with the work, and he gave her words. But look at the words. Allahu akbar: God is greater. Greater than the mill, the tiredness, whatever the day took out of you. And he didn't send it with a messenger. He came himself, at night, and sat on the edge of their bed to teach them. Ali said he never stopped saying it, not one night, even in the middle of a war. So the set that closes many Muslims' prayers, thirty-three, thirty-three, thirty-three or thirty-four, has a family story inside it. A tired daughter. A father at the bedside. A gift that doesn't wear out, costs nothing, and is there when the servant isn't.
screen: `FATIMAH ASKS FOR A SERVANT.` · `HE SITS DOWN BETWEEN THEM.` · `SOMETHING BETTER THAN WHAT YOU ASKED.` · `34, 33, 33, AT BEDTIME.` · then, large: `BETTER FOR YOU THAN A SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Whether you've just prayed or simply have two minutes, rest your right hand, palm up. Count the full hundred on your finger joints, twice around the hand and a little more for each: thirty-three of subhanallah, glory, thirty-three of alhamdulillah, praise, thirty-four of Allahu akbar, greater. If you don't pray, count the numbers, and on the last set, hold the thing that tired you most this week next to the words.
Allahu akbar. God is greater, thirty-four times, the last of the three, the gift given to Fatimah instead of a servant. Today's word.
Your line: better than a servant. Many still say Fatimah's hundred at bedtime. See you tomorrow.

117.title: La ilaha illallah
117.hook: the heaviest words on the scale, no god but Allah
117.howItsDone: Muslims say la ilaha illallah as dhikr after prayers and through the day, often counted on the fingers or beads, and hope it will be the last words on their lips before death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Allahu akbar, thirty-four, the gift to Fatimah. Your line was better than a servant. Today, one sentence on a scale.

A scale, the old kind, two pans hanging from a beam. On one side: ninety-nine scrolls, records of things they did wrong, each one, the story says, stretching as far as the eye can see. The pan crashes down. On the other side, someone places one small card, a few words written on it. The scale swings the other way. The scrolls fly up. The card is heavier. It's a hadith, in the collection of at-Tirmidhi. Today: the words on the card.
screen: `NINETY-NINE SCROLLS.` → `ONE SMALL CARD.` → `THE CARD IS HEAVIER.`

segments.voice: On the card is the testimony of faith, and its heart is the first half: la ilaha illallah. There is no god but Allah. Saying it is called tahlil. You've met these words inside the shahada, the first pillar, in the call to prayer, and at the end of the hundred after the prayer, three days ago. But look at how the sentence is built. It starts with a no. La ilaha: there is no god. Every idol, cleared away first. Some teachers read it more widely: anything a person serves without calling it worship, like money or approval. Then, illallah: except Allah. Only one comes back. Scholars call the two halves the negation and the affirmation. You empty the room, then let one in. The Qur'an puts the same idea in Surah al-Ikhlas, four short verses, which in Pickthall's translation reads: "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him." A hadith in Tirmidhi calls la ilaha illallah the best remembrance. One in Abu Dawud says that whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter Paradise. And that's the point of the card. Ninety-nine scrolls of mistakes, and one sentence underneath them all: I knew there was only one. In the tradition, that sentence, meant truly, weighs more than all the rest.
screen: `TAHLIL — NO GOD BUT ALLAH.` · `FIRST, A NO.` · `THEN ONE COMES BACK.` · `SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE.` · then, large: `THE CARD OUTWEIGHS THE SCROLLS.`

segments.voice: Say it ten times, slowly, counting on your fingers: on la ilaha, breathe out and let go of one thing that takes up more of your mind than it should; on illallah, breathe in. If you pray, say the Arabic; if you don't, breathe the shape of it, out, letting go, in, one thing left. Then rest the hand and stay quiet.
Tahlil. Saying la ilaha illallah, there is no god but Allah: a no that clears the room, and a yes. Today's word.
Your line: there is only one. Everything else can go back in its place. Day one hundred seventeen, done.

118.title: Astaghfirullah, a hundred times
118.hook: asking forgiveness a hundred times a day, as he did (Muslim)
118.howItsDone: Muslims say astaghfirullah three times right after finishing each prayer, and many repeat it through the day, sometimes a hundred times, following the Prophet's example.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tahlil, la ilaha illallah, the card that outweighs the scrolls. Your line was there is only one. Today, a word said a hundred times a day.

How many times did you say sorry yesterday? Maybe a dozen. Sorry, bumped your cart. Sorry, running late. Sorry, can you say that again? Most of those aren't really apologies; they're grease on the gears of the day. How many times did you really ask to be forgiven? Maybe once. Maybe not at all. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ tells the people: O people, turn to Allah in repentance, for I turn to Him a hundred times a day. A hundred.
screen: `A DOZEN SORRYS A DAY.` → `HOW MANY REAL ONES?` → `A HUNDRED TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: The word is astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness. Saying it is called istighfar. The root, gh-f-r, means to cover, to shield; Arabic dictionaries list a soldier's helmet, mighfar, from the same root. So forgiveness, in this picture, isn't just wiping a slate. It's being covered, protected from what the mistake would otherwise do. Now the surprise. Muslims generally hold that the Prophet was protected from serious sin, though the schools describe that protection differently. So why ask forgiveness a hundred times a day? Scholars give a few answers. Some say humility: the closer a person is to God, the more they notice the distance. Some say teaching: he did it so his community would. A version of the hadith says: something covers my heart, a kind of cloud, and I ask forgiveness a hundred times a day. In Bukhari, the number is more than seventy. And it's not only about sins. Istighfar is said three times at the end of the prayer, right after the taslim, as if to say: I tried, and it wasn't perfect. The Qur'an adds a promise. In Surah Nuh, the prophet Nuh tells his people: ask forgiveness of your Lord, and He will send rain, and help you with wealth and sons, and give you gardens and rivers. Asking forgiveness, paired with rain. There's also a longer form, the master of all istighfar, reported in Bukhari. But the short one, one word, is the one people carry all day.
screen: `GH-F-R — TO COVER, TO SHIELD.` · `WHY WOULD HE NEED IT?` · `THREE TIMES, AFTER THE PRAYER.` · `ASK, AND THE RAIN COMES.` · then, large: `A HUNDRED TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Rest your right hand, palm up. If you pray, say astaghfirullah on each finger joint, not rushing, and let a face or a moment come to mind now and then, something you'd like covered; if you don't, say sorry silently on each count, and mean some of them. Go slowly; you won't reach a hundred, and that's fine.
Istighfar. Saying astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness; to be covered and shielded, a hundred times a day. Today's word.
Your line: I ask forgiveness. One word, and a cover. That's day one hundred eighteen.

119.title: Prayers on the Prophet ﷺ
119.hook: sending blessings on him, returned tenfold (Muslim)
119.howItsDone: Muslims say sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam whenever the Prophet is named, recite the prayer of blessings on Muhammad and Ibrahim in the last sitting of every prayer, and many increase their salawat on Fridays.

segments.voice: Yesterday: istighfar, astaghfirullah, to be covered and shielded. Your line was I ask forgiveness.

Every time the Prophet's name has appeared on your screen on this path, it's been followed by a small symbol, a knot of Arabic calligraphy. Maybe you wondered what it was. This week's words have mostly been for God. Today's is still addressed to God, but it asks for someone else. Today: what that little symbol says.
screen: `A SMALL SYMBOL AFTER HIS NAME.` → `A KNOT OF CALLIGRAPHY.` → `WHAT DOES IT SAY?`

segments.voice: The symbol is short for sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam: may Allah send blessings on him and peace. Saying it, or any prayer like it, is called salawat, the plural of salah, the same word as prayer. It's said when his name is spoken. Why? The Qur'an, in Surah al-Ahzab, says that Allah and His angels send blessings on the Prophet, and tells the believers: you, too, send blessings on him, and greet him with peace. So a Muslim who says it is joining something already happening. The companions took this seriously enough to ask how. A hadith in Bukhari says they came to him: we know how to greet you with peace, but how do we send blessings on you? He taught them a prayer that begins: O Allah, send blessings on Muhammad and on the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings on Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim. Many Muslims recite it in the last sitting of every prayer, just before the peace to both sides. Notice who's in it: Ibrahim, the friend of God, whose story you met in camp two. Then the promise. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet said: whoever sends one blessing on me, Allah sends ten blessings on them. One goes out, ten come back. And a gentle rebuke. A hadith in Tirmidhi says the stingy one is the person who hears my name and doesn't send a blessing. Four words in Arabic, and holding them back earns that name.
screen: `SALLALLAHU 'ALAYHI WA SALLAM.` · `ALLAH AND HIS ANGELS SEND BLESSINGS.` · `AS YOU BLESSED IBRAHIM.` · `ONE GOES OUT, TEN COME BACK.` · then, large: `THE STINGY ONE HEARS AND IS SILENT.`

segments.voice: Rest your right hand, palm up, and count ten salawat, slowly: ten, not a hundred. If you pray, say sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam on each count, or the longer prayer from the last sitting if you know it; if you don't, hold in mind the man the words are for, sent, Muslims say, as a mercy to the worlds, and count ten breaths.
Salawat. Blessings sent on the Prophet, the words behind the symbol; one sent, ten returned. Today's word, and a week of remembrance on your fingers.
Your line: peace on him. Tomorrow, the path turns to a month: Ramadan, and the new moon. Day one hundred nineteen.
